newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK people mourn Deng with tea and cigarettes.
newsitem.headline: HK people mourn Deng with tea and cigarettes.

text.p: Hong Kong people streamed to pay tribute to the late Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping at Beijing's mission in the territory on Monday, laying offerings ranging from cigarettes and tea to books at a temporary shrine.
In the five days since Deng died aged 92, some 35,000 men, women and children have visited the shrine at the Xinhua News Agency, China's de facto embassy near Hong Kong's Happy Valley racecourse.
"He liked smoking and drinking tea," said one 73-year-old man after presenting his offering of cigarettes and tea from Deng's native Sichuan province in southwestern China.
Another mourner laid down a book about Hong Kong, the cover featuring a photographic panorama of the territory, placing his business card with it.

It was Deng who directed negotiations with London for the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule after a century and a half as a British colony. He died just months before China's red flag is finally hoisted in the territory, at midnight on June 30.
Mourners, some wearing a white flower on their chest to symbolise grief, placed bouquets at a shrine already stacked with countless wreaths from Hong Kong dignitaries.
A group of nursery infants, accompanied by their teacher, paid their respects to the late Chinese leader, holding a banner that said "Mr Deng is immortal".
Some of the mourners failed to hold back their tears as they bowed before Deng's photograph. Others shook hands with the grieving Chinese officials on duty at the scene.

Big queues formed outside the Xinhua building on Monday, the final day of the memorial vigil there. Sources at Xinhua said more than 5,000 people -- from all walks of life -- paid their respects on Monday morning alone.
This was in addition to about 30,000 mourners who had flocked there on the previous four days, a Xinhua official said.

Some in the queue refused to waste the waiting time, jabbering into their mobile phones about business deals or scanning the business newspapers -- essential activities in this bustling financial centre.
Chinese-funded companies encouraged staff to pay their respects to Deng by giving them special time off.
"Uncle Deng did so much for us. He made a great contribution to Hong Kong and China," said a woman in her twenties working for a Chinese bank.
